newsitem.title: FRANCE: True North gets own Euro agency.
newsitem.headline: True North gets own Euro agency.

text.p: True North Communication's accord with Publicis, announced after over a year of discord, brings the U.S. firm a European network it controls totally, True North's international president said on Thursday.

"We have got our own 100 percent managed network in Europe which we haven't had for the last 10 years," Harry Reid, president of True North Communications International, told Reuters in a telephone interview.
Publicis earlier said it had settled all outstanding differences with True North and would transfer the FCB agencies in Paris, London, Lisbon and Athens to True North.

True North said in a statement that following the accord with Publicis, it will form a new Foote, Cone & Belding (FCB) European network by uniting the four FCB offices which were formerly part of the Publicis/FCB joint venture with Wilkens International, the 19-country pan-European advertising network it bought on January 31.

"The combination of our European FCB units and Wilkens results in a full-service pan-European network with billings surpassing $1 billion and with more than 850 employees," the statement quoted Brendan Ryan, chairman and chief executive of Foote, Cone & Belding, as saying.

Under the accord, Publicis will own the rest of the FCB European venture not transferred to True North, and True North will transfer to Publicis "a portion" of its 49 percent stake in Publicis FCB. The remainder will be converted to give True North 26.5 percent of Publicis Communication, Publicis SA's advertising operating unit, up from 20.8 percent previously.
Publicis will maintain its 20 percent stake in True North and will be its largest shareholder. Both companies will hold a seat on each others' board of directors.
"It's a very agreeable restatement of our working partnership with Publicis," Reid said.
The link between the two advertising groups goes back to 1988. A year ago the two publicly admitted they were talking about renewing their alliance after Publicis ended their original agreements.

True North itself had been going through a transition period in which Foote, Cone & Belding, the largest U.S. agency in terms of billings, suffered a major setback with the loss of the Colgate global ad account to Young & Rubicam in 1995, and some doubts over True North's international clout.
FCB won back credibility since then with a string of major gains, including the $400 million SC Johnson account.
In November True North chairman Bruce Mason said 1997 looked as if it would be a good year for the firm.
The advertising trade press was full of speculation of new alliances for True North and Publicis, and played up the discord between the two.
But True North's Reid said reports of acrimony were overdone.
"Some of the acrimony has been very inaccurate. The partnership in terms of client service has been fantastic... it hasn't been World War Three for sure," he said.

The disagreement dates back more than a year, prompted by a feeling on both sides that certain aspects of the agreement had been broken and "something had happened to the spirit of partnership," Reid said.
Both companies are now free to forge whatever alliances they wish to, he added in response to questions.
The continuing link between True North and Publicis will still serve both groups in particular ways, he said.
True North will have ongoing financial revenue from its Publicis stake, and the alliance will show its fruits in particular markets like media buying, where size is becoming important, he said.
Publicis, which is just starting up its international network, will still be able to call on True North for servicing in places where it has not yet set up its own agency, he said.
-- Sue Landau, Paris news room +33 1 4221 5452
